prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Based on my research of the provided sources, here are the official statements from the Python Software Foundation and CPython developers regarding the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build:

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "the performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft's Faster CPython team, or Meta's Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it's more like 3%)." | CLAIM: Current performance overhead is approximately 10% on most platforms, with lower overhead on macOS

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance)." | CLAIM: Memory usage increases by 15-20% in free-threaded builds

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for `--disable-gil` builds." | CLAIM: There is measurable execution overhead in no-GIL builds

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The largest contribution to execution overhead is biased reference counting followed by per-object locking." | CLAIM: The main sources of overhead are biased reference counting and per-object locking mechanisms

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Performance overhead varies by platform, with lower overhead on macOS ARM systems

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build." | CLAIM: Memory usage is generally higher in free-threaded builds

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "At this point we're expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Steering Council expects worst-case performance penalty of 10-15%

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code." | CLAIM: Performance impact is limited to free-threaded builds only

The sources consistently show that while there is a performance and memory overhead in free-threaded builds (typically 5-15% CPU overhead and 15-20% memory overhead), this overhead is considered acceptable given the benefits of true parallelism, and it only affects the free-threaded build while leaving the traditional GIL-enabled build unaffected.
